strengths: Well-motivated neuroscience-inspired approach to agent-environment disentanglement
Self-supervised method removes need for explicit agent masks required by prior work
Comprehensive experimental coverage with real-world (BAIR) and simulated (Meta-world) validation
Detailed reproducibility information including hyperparameters, architecture details, and computational requirements
Demonstrates positive results on several tasks, including achieving 100% success rate on some manipulation tasks across random seeds
weaknesses: Insufficient statistical rigor: only 3 random seeds per experiment, acknowledged by authors as inadequate for statistical significance; results could easily be within noise
Efficiency gains are overstated: 50k-step motor-babbling requirement represents significant computational overhead that negates claimed 23% efficiency improvements
Inconsistent and modest improvements: 8% performance gain is marginal; sample efficiency is best in only 6/10 tasks, with method underperforming baselines on some tasks
Limited novelty: scene encoder architecture borrowed from prior work; uses standard loss functions (L2 reconstruction, similarity loss); primarily an application of existing techniques
Core claims lack rigorous validation: no quantitative disentanglement metrics; degraded video prediction quality when jointly training with RL undermines mechanism being exploited
Narrow experimental scope: only simple robotic manipulation tasks; single robot in BAIR dataset; generalization to different agents and domains unclear

Hyperparameter sensitivity: authors used non-optimized values for β and H; Figures 2 and 9 show non-trivial parameter dependence; theoretical justification for why motor prediction regularizes RL is missing

Overstated claims: assertion about 'removing supervision' is misleading since motor babbling is itself a form of training signal; efficiency gains offset by babbling overhead not fully accounted for in metrics

strengths: Well-motivated neuroscientific grounding with compelling intuition for motor prediction
Removes supervision requirement compared to SEAR, improving practical applicability
Comprehensive two-track evaluation on both real-world (BAIR) and simulated (Meta-world) domains
Excellent reproducibility: detailed architectures, hyperparameters, computational requirements, and code release promised
Clear presentation with well-designed figures and smooth exposition
Includes ablation studies on key hyperparameters (β and prediction horizon)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: directly reuses Denton & Birodkar (2017) architecture and similarity loss; core contribution is straightforward application of auxiliary loss regularization, which is well-explored

Modest empirical improvements: only 8% average performance gain and 23% efficiency gain measured by loose metric; many NA baseline values; only 3 random seeds insufficient for statistical significance
Motor-babbling requirement of 50k steps directly contradicts sample-efficiency claims and represents hard constraint undermining a core motivation

Weak real-world evaluation: BAIR disentanglement analysis is primarily qualitative with no quantitative metrics; acknowledged incompleteness ('can't completely disentangle'); single handcrafted example for generalization

Unclear mechanistic understanding: paper claims prediction 'regularizes' RL but provides no formal justification or comparison to other auxiliary tasks; connection between disentanglement quality and RL improvement assumed rather than demonstrated
Limited evaluation scope: single robot morphology (Sawyer), only 10 Meta-world tasks, no diverse embodiments despite generalization motivation
Problematic baseline comparisons: SEAR uses supervision while DrQ-v2 doesn't, conflating different problem settings; inconsistent missing values in Table 1
Joint training degrades reconstruction quality compared to BAIR-only training, suggesting conflicting objectives, yet authors dismiss this concern without adequate justification

Design choices lack justification: reconstruction only on last timestep, ad-hoc random time gap for similarity loss, different architectures for BAIR vs Meta-world, unjustified train-test distribution shift (2→28 frames)
Non-optimized hyperparameters (β, H) acknowledged by authors, suggesting suboptimal results and undermining improvement claims

strengths: Well-motivated neuroscience-inspired approach to agent-environment disentanglement that is intuitive and clearly presented
Practical contribution: removes requirement for supervisory agent masks, making the method more widely applicable than SEAR
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including real-world BAIR dataset, 10 diverse Meta-world tasks, appropriate baselines, and ablation studies

Consistent improvements on majority of tasks (5/10 wins) with notably narrow success ranges suggesting reliable behavior; qualitative results (Figure 8) effectively demonstrate learned disentanglement
Excellent reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, architecture specifications, computational resources disclosed, code promised
Clear presentation with effective motivation and well-structured narrative; good use of figures to illustrate concepts
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: architecture (DCGAN-based), similarity loss (Denton & Birodkar 2017), and reconstruction loss are standard; primary contribution is combining existing components as auxiliary RL objective

Motor-babbling overhead (50k steps) substantially undermines efficiency claims—in Door Close/Lock tasks, improvements only materialize after babbling, negating efficiency gains; 50k cost not included in efficiency comparisons

Experimental validation incomplete: only 3 random seeds (insufficient for statistical significance), only DDPG tested (generalization to PPO/SAC unclear), no real robot experiments, hyperparameters acknowledged as non-optimized

Disentanglement claims not rigorously validated: only qualitative visual results provided, no quantitative disentanglement metrics; acknowledged blurring of objects suggests imperfect separation; no evidence that disentanglement quality correlates with RL gains

Regularization mechanism underspecified: theoretical justification for why predictability regularizes learning is weak; multiple mechanisms plausible but not isolated through ablations; Figure 2 shows effect but doesn't validate hypothesis

Improvements modest and inconsistent: 8% average performance gain masks high variance (some +30%, others 0%-negative); efficiency improvements in only 6/10 tasks, with method failing on Bin Picking/Assembly without explanation; 3-seed runs make statistical significance unclear

strengths: Clear motivation rooted in cognitive science (body schema development) for learning agent-aware representations
Simple, practical approach that can be applied on top of existing model-free RL algorithms without major modifications
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 3 simulated benchmarks and real-world data, with effective visualizations demonstrating feature disentanglement
Thorough ablation study examining key hyperparameters and their effects on performance
Good reproducibility with detailed architectural and training specifications
Addresses practical challenges like preventing goal-directed exploration through motor babbling
weaknesses: Limited novelty given recent concurrent/prior work on agent-environment disentanglement in RL (Gmelin et al. 2023, Qian et al. 2025); key distinctions from this work are not clearly articulated
Mixed experimental results with inconsistent improvements; performance gains are sometimes modest and within noise margins; method underperforms Dreamer-v3 on some tasks
Missing direct comparison with Gmelin et al. (2023), the most relevant prior work on this exact topic
Lacks theoretical justification for why agent-environment disentanglement improves RL performance or convergence guarantees
Real-world evaluation limited to qualitative predictions on handcrafted trajectories with no quantitative RL evaluation on actual robots
Multiple hyperparameters introduced (β, l_ha, prediction horizon, babbling duration) with limited justification for specific choices; computational overhead unquantified
Limited environment diversity—all simulated tasks are vision-based robotic manipulation/locomotion; no evaluation on other RL domains (e.g., Atari, other continuous control)
No analysis of when agent-environment disentanglement helps vs. hurts; limited discussion of failure modes and why method underperforms on some benchmarks
Missing ablation studies separating contribution of agent-environment split from general auxiliary learning; no comparison with simpler baseline auxiliary losses

strengths: Well-motivated approach grounded in neuroscience principles of learning body self-models through motion prediction
Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning multiple simulated benchmarks (Meta-World, Distracting DMC, Hurdle DMC) and real-world data (BAIR dataset)
Reasonable architectural design combining encoder-decoder with recurrent dynamics prediction for agent feature learning
Includes ablation studies on key hyperparameters (prediction weight β, horizon, feature dimensionality, babbling stage)
Provides visualization of learned agent vs. environment features (Figures 4-5) showing some interpretability
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Agent-environment disentanglement is well-explored in literature. The core contribution—using motion prediction for disentanglement in model-free RL—is relatively incremental over existing work (Gmelin et al. 2023, Qian et al. 2025, etc.)

Marginal and inconsistent improvements: Figure 6 shows many Meta-World tasks with DRQv2-EF performing similarly to or worse than Dreamer-v3. Figure 7 shows mixed results on Distracting/Hurdle DMC, with large overlapping error bars suggesting improvements are within noise

Non-standard evaluation methodology in Section 4.3: The custom 'sample-efficiency and performance' score using 85%/90%/95% thresholds is unconventional and appears designed to favor the method. No statistical significance testing (p-values, confidence intervals) provided

Missing critical ablations: No ablation separating motion prediction alone from the full disentanglement approach. Cannot isolate whether improvements come from the auxiliary loss, bottleneck design, or added model capacity

Insufficient validation of core claims: The paper's central claim about learning 'agent-aware representations' lacks rigor. Only visual inspection (Figure 4) provided; no quantitative disentanglement metrics (MIG, SAP, FactorVAE scores) computed. Unclear whether bottleneck enforces disentanglement or just compression

No theoretical justification: Lacks analysis of why motion prediction should improve RL policy learning or explanation of when this approach succeeds/fails. Connection between motion-predictable features and RL task performance assumed rather than established

Real-world results are only qualitative: Figure 5 (BAIR dataset) shows only visualizations with no quantitative metrics. The 'handcrafted trajectory' experiment is too simplistic to demonstrate real generalization

Technical design choices appear ad-hoc: (1) Motor-babbling requirement suggests instability of the base approach; (2) Pixel-level MSE reconstruction is suboptimal for visual tasks (perceptual losses not explored); (3) Episode partition design not justified; (4) Unclear why random action injection solves the problem
Unfair baseline comparison: SEAR uses supervisory agent mask from simulator while EF must learn motion prediction—this trade-off in information access is not discussed or accounted for

Limited experimental scope for reproducibility: Many hyperparameters appear to be tuned; sensitivity to choices unexplored. No code availability mentioned. Generalization to new embodiments untested. Different environments may require different hyperparameters

strengths: Well-motivated approach grounded in neuroscience and developmental psychology, using agent movement prediction to learn disentangled representations
Solid technical execution with clear architectural design separating agent and scene features, properly integrated with RL objectives
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across diverse domains (Meta-World, Distracting/Hurdle DMC, BAIR real-world dataset) with consistent aggregate improvements (17/20 Meta-World tasks)
Thoughtful ablation study examining key hyperparameters (β, H, l_h) and their effects on performance
Clear presentation with effective visualizations demonstrating disentanglement and task solutions
Real-world validation on BAIR dataset strengthens claims about practical applicability
weaknesses: Incremental novelty - the core concept of agent-environment disentanglement is well-established; the specific visuomotor formulation is novel but the overall contribution feels incremental relative to prior work (Gmelin et al. 2023, Kim & Mnih 2018)
Mixed results on some benchmarks (Hurdle DMC shows inconsistent improvements) with no clear guidance on when/why the method helps or hurts, suggesting domain sensitivity
Computational overhead from encoder, recurrent model, and decoder is not quantitatively analyzed; no wall-clock time comparisons provided despite mentioning overhead in conclusions
Limited baseline comparisons - primarily DrQ-v2 variants and SEAR (authors' prior work); missing comparisons with other recent agent-aware representation learning methods
Hyperparameter sensitivity without principled selection strategy - β, H, and l_h choices appear somewhat arbitrary with no guidance for practitioners on new tasks
Insufficient statistical analysis - no significance tests provided despite modest improvements on some tasks; confidence intervals would strengthen claims
Limited real-world validation to only BAIR dataset; handcrafted trajectory experiment is somewhat contrived; generalization claims need broader evidence
Quantitative disentanglement analysis lacking - Figure 1d visualization is qualitative; formal metrics (mutual information, SAP score) would strengthen claims about learning meaningful agent features
Reproducibility concerns - some implementation details missing (e.g., specific hyperparameter changes for Hurdle DMC), code availability not mentioned
Motor babbling stage introduced late (25000 steps) without sufficient upfront motivation for necessity
